fields.title: La migration du Burkina Faso vers le Nord de la Côte d’Ivoire face au changement climatique
fields.body:
**Contexte**

Plus de 4 millions de Burkinabè vivent en Côte d’Ivoire, témoignant d’une tradition migratoire parmi les plus ancrées d’Afrique de l’Ouest. La plupart s’inscrivent dans des trajectoires d’installation durable, souvent sur plusieurs générations. Depuis les années 1960, ces migrations ont soutenu le besoin de main-d’œuvre en Côte d’Ivoire, notamment dans l’agriculture. Elles suivent fréquemment des stratégies familiales où les hommes migrent en premier pour travailler avant d’être rejoints par leurs conjointes. Malgré un accès au foncier devenu plus contraignant depuis les années 1990, les opportunités économiques continuent d’attirer de nouveaux arrivant∙e∙s en Côte d’Ivoire, tandis que l’insécurité et les aléas climatiques au Burkina Faso contribuent de plus en plus aux départs.

Cette étude de cas vise à comprendre comment les changements climatiques influencent les parcours migratoires et l’installation des Burkinabè vivant dans le Nord de la Côte d’Ivoire. Elle s’appuie sur des entretiens qualitatifs avec 56 Burkinabè interrogé∙e∙s dans trois villes secondaires du district des Savanes ; Korhogo, Ouangolodougou et Ferkessédougou.

*La dégradation de l’environnement dans le Nord de la Côte d’Ivoire fragilise l’économie rurale, principale porte d’entrée économique des migrant∙e∙s burkinabè*

• Les Burkinabè interrogé∙e∙s décrivent une rupture entre un passé agricole en Côte d’Ivoire perçu comme prospère et une situation économique actuelle plus incertaine.

• Ils/elles rapportent une baisse des rendements agricoles associée à la dégradation de l’environnement, qu’ils/ elles expliquent par deux dynamiques qui sont liées

: Les changements dans le climat, notamment avec des pluies plus irrégulières et souvent insuffisantes, qui viennent perturber les cycles agricoles.

Les activités humaines, telles que la déforestation et la surexploitation des terres, qui contribuent à l’épuisement des sols et des ressources en eau.

• Les difficultés financières en Côte d’Ivoire s’accumulent. Les répondant∙e∙s peinent à couvrir leurs dépenses essentielles tandis que le risque d’endettement augmente. Leurs obligations sociales, telles que les transferts d’argent à la famille, deviennent plus difficiles à honorer.

• Les femmes sont plus vulnérables1 car elles occupent une position défavorable dans la chaîne de valeur agricole. Elles sont plus présentes dans les activités de transformation et de vente. Elles subissent donc simultanément la hausse des coûts des matières premières et la baisse de la consommation locale.

fields.title: Migration from Burkina Faso to northern Côte d’Ivoire in the context of climate change
fields.body:
## **What adaptation strategies are available for Burkinabè migrants working in the agricultural sector?**

This case study looks at migration from Burkina Faso. It aims to understand how climate change influences the migration patterns and settlement experiences of Burkinabè living in northern Côte d’Ivoire. The study draws on qualitative interviews with 56 Burkinabè respondents in Korhogo, Ouangolodougou and Ferkessédougou. These are three secondary cities in the Savanes district.

**Background**

More than 4 million people from Burkina Faso live in Côte d’Ivoire, reflecting one of the most deeply rooted traditions of migration in West Africa. Most follow patterns of long-term settlement, often spanning several generations. Since the 1960s, these migrations have helped meet the demand for labour in Côte d’Ivoire, particularly in agriculture.

## **Key findings**

- The Burkinabè interviewees describe **a contrast between** **what they perceive as a prosperous** **agricultural past in Côte d’Ivoire and a more uncertain current economic situation**.
- They report a **decline in agricultural yields linked to environmental degradation**, which they attribute to two interrelated factors: Climate change, notably increasingly **irregular and often** **insufficient rainfall**, which disrupts agricultural cycles and human activities, such as deforestation and overexploitation of land, which contribute to **declining soil fertility and the depletion of water resources**.
- **Financial difficulties in Côte d’Ivoire are mounting.** Respondents are struggling to cover essential expenses, whilst the risk of falling into debt is increasing.
- **Women are more vulnerable** **as they find themselves in an unfavourable position in the agricultural value chain.** They are more heavily involved in processing and sales. They are therefore simultaneously affected by rising costs of primary agricultural products and declining local consumption.

fields.title: Anticipated El Niño Impacts on Water Resources and Water Infrastructure in Somalia: Technical Brief, September 2026
fields.body:
**Executive summary**

**AT A GLANCE**

El Niño is under way and strengthening: NOAA gives a greater than 90 percent chanceof a very strong event, and ICPAC a 90 percent probability of above-normal October–December rainfall over central and southern Somalia. Against that outlook, all 7,517strategic water sources in FAO-SWALIM's and MoEWR national inventory werescreened for flood exposure. 507 lie in areas of confirmed historical inundation; afurther 97 are supported as exposed by two or more independent lines of evidence. 71sources are classified Very high risk and 524 High risk, including 68 of the strategicboreholes that SWALIM and FMS MoEWR monitors weekly. Ten districts hold 65percent of the at-risk stock. Protective works cost roughly 7 percent of the correctiveand emergency response they displace and must be financed in September to bedelivered before the rains.

**The forecast, and its confidence**

El Niño is present and intensifying, and the forecasting centres agree to an unusual degree.NOAA's ENSO Diagnostic Discussion of 13 August 2026 maintains an El Niño Advisory on aJuly Niño-3.4 anomaly of +1.4 °C and gives a greater than 90 percent chance of a very strongevent through the 2026-27 northern winter; IRI puts El Niño probability at 100 percent throughearly 2027; ICPAC gives a 90 percent probability of above-normal October–December rainfallover central and southern Somalia, with totals above 400 mm and a likely positive Indian OceanDipole. FEWS NET expects September–November rainfall above 120 percent of average withan early onset and carries an explicit risk of Famine (IPC Phase 5) in riverine and agropastoralareas should flooding be extreme. Table 1 records each position with its issue date.

The ENSO and seasonal rainfall signals are high confidence. The translation from a three-monthregional rainfall anomaly to inundation at a specific water point is not, and is treated throughoutthis report as a scenario rather than a forecast. Above-normal seasonal rainfall does not by itselfplace a borehole under water.

fields.title: Israel’s Genocide in Gaza Persists One Year into the So-Called “Ceasefire”
fields.body:
A year ago, on October 10, 2025, a ceasefire agreement in the Gaza Strip was announced. For a moment, we at PHRI had a glimpse of hope that this would bring relief and rehabilitation to Palestinians and allow the recovery and reconstruction of the decimated healthcare system.

The analysis we’re releasing today exposes Israel’s continued prevention of any meaningful recovery of Gaza’s healthcare system.

In July 2025, PHRI concluded that Israeli authorities were responsible for committing the crime of genocide by deliberately inflicting conditions of life calculated to bring about the destruction of the Palestinian population in Gaza.

We have continued since to monitor shortages of medical supplies disrupting healthcare services, shortages in diagnostics and treatment, and limited medical evacuations for critical patients in need of lifesaving treatment outside of the Strip. Since October 2025, PHRI has followed more than a dozen cases of children who died while awaiting medical evacuation, as Israel blocks the medical corridor between Gaza and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem.

In the summer of 2026, PHRI received a list of acute deficits and depleted stocks of medical equipment from the Gaza Ministry of Health. A comparison with the list received a year earlier shows that shortages have not eased during the ceasefire and had, in some cases, increased. The situation on the ground speaks for itself: on October 2, Nasser Medical Complex ran out of syringes.

Yet raw aid volume and truck counts are misleading metrics. What matters is whether Palestinians in Gaza have access to the conditions necessary to sustain a healthy and dignified life, including functioning hospitals, essential medicines and medical equipment, and lifesaving treatment.

One year into the ceasefire, the continued destruction and denial of these conditions, in the absence of accountability, means that Israel’s genocide in Gaza persists.

**We demand that Israeli authorities immediately restore the medical corridor between the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, lift all restrictions on the entry of aid, including medicines, medical equipment, and humanitarian personnel, and allow meaningful reconstruction of Gaza’s healthcare system and civilian infrastructure.**

fields.title: Democratic Republic of the Congo Country Report: The State Of the Humanitarian System 2026
fields.body:
**EXECUTIVE SUMMARY**

This country report for the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) provides an evidence-based overview of the current international humanitarian system between 2022 and 2025 to supplement the global analysis in [The State of the Humanitarian System 2026 (SOHS)](https://alnap.org/sohs/). It describes the country’s humanitarian context and responses to ongoing crises; outlines the size, shape and performance of the humanitarian system; and highlights key findings from primary research in North and South Kivu, supplemented with secondary data including scholarly and grey literature. The country report offers a comprehensive picture of how the international humanitarian system, alongside other actors, operates in DRC and it assesses the system’s effectiveness in meeting the needs of people affected by conflict and crises.

Our research indicates a mixed picture of the state of the humanitarian system in DRC, with several important challenges. Improvements include better delivery of aid in line with internationally recognised standards in more accessible areas, as well as greater preparedness and capacity among skilled staff to respond to the needs of populations affected by crisis. Humanitarian actors are also increasingly adapting their operational approaches to better support community needs. However, several structural challenges continue to hinder the effectiveness of the humanitarian system in DRC. The system remains heavily dominated by United Nations (UN) agencies and international organisations, who control funding, resources and agenda-setting processes, often to the detriment of local and national actors, as well as people affected by crisis. Other challenges include access, ensuring accountability to affected people, and widespread sexual abuse and exploitation.

The power imbalance between international and local actors – with international actors holding a near-monopoly over decision-making power – combined with limited government engagement, creates an environment in which humanitarian actors operate with excessive autonomy and a laissez-faire, hands-off approach. This situation is further reinforced by a lack of transparency, weak accountability mechanisms, political influence and insufficient action to address other forms of misconduct. There remains limited progress on localisation, and practices such as gatekeeping continue to negatively affect adherence to humanitarian principles. In this context, some aid workers exploit these systemic weaknesses to engage in corrupt practices, diversion of humanitarian assistance and other forms of misconduct, including sexual exploitation and abuse and other practices that undermine the dignity of aid recipients.

Corruption and aid diversion take many forms and represent some of the most critical setbacks in the humanitarian system in eastern DRC. They are both structural and systemic, sometimes involving well-organised networks and actors who are supposed to prevent and combat these excesses. Together, these challenges undermine the effectiveness of humanitarian interventions and erode the sector’s overall credibility and trustworthiness.

Organisations have adapted through local partnerships and by modifying modalities, but assistance has not met needs. Prioritisation has focused narrowly on survival, leaving critical sectors such as protection and psychosocial support underserved.

At the household level, aid has been inconsistent and poorly adapted to prolonged displacement, with uneven targeting and the exclusion of vulnerable groups. Consequently, trust has declined, resource competition has increased and social tensions have grown.

**Recommendations**

Decision-makers, humanitarian stakeholders and practitioners need to promote good practices of humanitarian assistance. This includes:

- developing mechanisms that promote transparency and social accountability in all steps of assistance, including verification mechanisms that specifically target local chiefs and aid camps in coordination with aid frontline staff
- promoting protection and dignity, including preventing and combating sexual exploitation and abuse
- working to shift decision-making power to national and local humanitarian actors, as well as para-humanitarian stakeholders
- proactive preparedness for epidemics and outbreaks
- prioritising services in collaboration with local communities, where replacement funds cannot be secured.

fields.title: Central African Republic - Key Message Update: Crisis persists in conflict-affected areas despite the gradual end of the lean season, September 2026 - January 2027
fields.body:
**Key Messages**

- **Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected to persist through January 2027 in the areas most affected by insecurity and isolation, particularly Vakaga, Haute-Kotto, Haut-Mbomou, as well as parts of the northwest.** Despite the seasonal improvement expected from October onward in the north, below-average production and livelihoods constrained by insecurity, high prices, and low purchasing power will continue to limit food access. Clashes, displacement, mobility restrictions, and tensions related to [**transhumance**](https://www.journaldebangui.com/rca-pres-de-2-700-personnes-deplacees-apres-le-meurtre-dun-eleveur-a-batangafo/) will continue to disrupt agricultural activities, livelihoods, and access to markets. Households will increasingly resort to reducing the number of meals, taking on debt, and selling assets to meet their food needs. In contrast, in Bamingui-Bangoran, the decline in conflict-related incidents and improved access to fields and forest resources are expected to support an improvement to Stressed (IPC Phase 2) in October.
- **From September through January 2027, Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes are expected to continue to predominate in several prefectures in the central, southern, and southwestern parts of the country, particularly Ouaka, Basse-Kotto, and Nana-Mambéré.** In these relatively more stable areas, maize and groundnut harvests, which have been underway since August, are gradually improving food availability and reducing households’ reliance on markets. Cassava, which is available year-round, also contributes to food access. In addition, income from seasonal agricultural activities supports the livelihoods of poor households. Most of these households are expected to be able to meet their essential food needs without heavy reliance on negative coping strategies. However, in Haut-Mbomou, persistent insecurity continues to limit access to fields, hunting, fishing, and gathering, exposing the most affected households to more severe difficulties in accessing food and income.
- **Agroclimatic conditions observed during the first 10 days of September remain favorable for crop development across most of the country.** Cumulative rainfall observed since the beginning of the season has generally been average to above average, with [**localized deficits**](https://data.chc.ucsb.edu/products/Early_Estimates/v3/Recent_Rainfall/observed/moving_18pentad/africa_west/pngs/archive/POA_18PentAccum_2026_p50.png) in the northeast, northwest, and southeast. In the central and southern areas, maize, groundnut, and rice harvesting has already begun or is nearing completion following the August/September start and generally satisfactory growing conditions. In the north, millet and sorghum crops are continuing to mature, and the main harvests are expected from October onward. Production prospects remain generally average in relatively stable areas, in line with estimates from the [**Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)**](https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country/CAF/pdf/CAF.pdf). However, limited access to agricultural inputs, as well as localized security constraints, will continue to restrict production levels in some affected areas.
- **Prices of major cereals remained high in August, particularly in isolated areas and areas affected by insecurity in the northeast.** In August, the price of maize in Birao (514 FCFA/kilogram) was approximately twice as high as in Bangui (257 FCFA/kilogram), reflecting [**persistent supply constraints**](https://reliefweb.int/report/central-african-republic/republique-centrafricaine-initiative-conjointe-de-suivi-des-marches-icsm-aout-septembre-2026?utm_source=rw-subscriptions&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=country_updates_54) and high transportation costs. Continued [**fuel shortages**](https://www.journaldebangui.com/rca-bangui-confrontee-a-une-nouvelle-penurie-de-carburant/) in September are expected to disrupt market supplies and trade flows, contributing to persistently high transportation costs and higher prices for imported food commodities. However, ongoing maize, groundnut, and rice harvests in several areas of the central, western, and southern parts of the country are expected to gradually improve market supplies and contribute to a seasonal decline in prices in relatively stable areas. In contrast, difficulties accessing markets in areas affected by insecurity and isolation are expected to keep prices relatively high.

fields.title: Mali - Key Message Update: Elevated food assistance needs persist in areas of Kidal and Ménaka in Emergency, September 2026 - January 2027
fields.body:
**Key Messages**

- **Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes persist in Kidal and Ménaka** due to major disruptions to trade flows, livelihoods, and access to food. **In Ménaka, an improvement to Crisis (IPC Phase 3) is expected from October onward** due to limited harvests and improved trade flows, despite consumption deficits. In Kidal, however, Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes are expected to persist amid severe reductions in food availability and access. In both regions, a proportion of households will remain in Emergency (IPC Phase 4) or even Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5) due to significant food consumption deficits. **In insecure areas of Gao, Mopti, and Tomboctou, outcomes are expected to improve from Crisis (IPC Phase 3) to Stressed (IPC Phase 2) starting in October** due to harvests and seasonal price reductions.
- **The progress of the agricultural season varies across areas due to the poor spatiotemporal rainfall.** Rainfall since the beginning of the season through mid-September has been [**below average**](https://edcintl.cr.usgs.gov/downloads/sciweb1/shared/fews/web/africa/west/pentadal/chirps/seasaccum/maysep/pctn/lta/graphics/wa_chirps_seasaccum_pctn_maysep_202653_lta.png) across the country, except in parts of Kita, Kayes, Nioro, Nara, and Sikasso, as well as certain parts of Ménaka and Tomboctou, where rainfall has been normal to above average. This rainfall deficit has hindered crop development, causing water stress and crop drying in several localities, particularly in Mopti, Douentza, Bandiagara, San, Ségou, Tomboctou, and Gao, where production declines are expected. Despite forecasts for [**average rainfall**](https://fews.net/global/seasonal-forecast-monthly-briefing/september-2026/print) from September to November, rainfall constraints, limited access to agricultural inputs, and reduced cultivated areas in insecure zones are negatively affecting the country's production prospects.
- **Security incidents continue to disrupt the movement of people and goods and market functioning, resulting in deteriorating household livelihoods and population displacement.** The security environment remains marked by recent attacks by Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) and the Front de Libération de l’Azawad (FLA) in the regions of Kidal and [**Mopti**](https://www.lequotidien.re/article/national-et-international/2026/09/18/nouveau-bilan-d-une-attaque-jihadiste-au-mali-au-moins-100-militaires-tues-sources-concordantes-doc-c8qm3nq), including ambushes targeting military convoys, the use of suicide drones, and repression of civilian populations, indicating an increase in [**operational capacity**](https://africacenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Worsening-Security-In-Mali-fr.pdf). In response, intensified military operations, particularly in the northern and central parts of the country, are continuing through airstrikes conducted by the army with support from its allies. These incidents are displacing populations and disrupting trade, mobility, and livestock movements, particularly in Kidal and Ménaka.
- **Market supplies of cereals remain sufficient despite reduced supply due to producers and traders withholding stocks in anticipation of unfavorable agricultural production prospects.** Cereal prices in mid-September remained generally stable compared with the previous month, although atypical increases were recorded in some localities in the central regions: Mopti (30 percent), Douentza (30 percent), Hombori (40 percent), Koro (50 percent), and Bankass (50 percent), due to poor production prospects expected in these areas. At the end of August, staple cereal prices were near or below the five-year average in all regions, except in Ménaka and Kidal, where prices were more than 10 percent above average. This is limiting poor households' access to food amid declining incomes and heavy reliance on markets.
- **Imports of essential goods, including fuel, are improving due to reduced disruptions along certain routes and increased use of the Abidjan-Bamako corridor, secured by regular military escorts.** This [**improvement**](https://www.govserv.org/ML/Quartier-du-Fleuve/110751465379012/Direction-G%C3%A9n%C3%A9rale--Commerce%2C--Consommation-%26--Concurrence#google_vignette) has enabled more regular fuel supplies and the gradual resumption of economic activities, particularly in cities and industrial facilities. However, imports remain below normal levels because of persistent difficulties along the Dakar-Bamako corridor. Some areas, particularly in central Mali, continue to experience [**irregular fuel supplies**](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260903-mali-carburant-et-%C3%A9lectricit%C3%A9-sont-disponibles-%C3%A0-bamako-la-fourniture-reste-erratique-dans-le-pays?utm_source=TheSahelBrief&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=sahel-morning-brief-3-september-2026). Despite the improvements observed, fuel availability in rural areas remains limited, with prices above the official price, increasing the costs of economic activities, including agricultural activities. In addition, [**the prolonged container immobilization**](https://fr.apanews.net/security/mali-les-conteneurs-vides-inquietent-les-chargeurs/) will disrupt the logistics chain and increase transportation costs, leading to higher prices for imported food commodities.
- **Livestock conditions are below average due to insufficient rainfall, which has limited pasture production**, resulting in [**moderate to severe pasture deficits**](https://agrhymet.cilss.int/2026/09/08/campagne-pastorale-2026-2027-des-deficits-fourragers-et-des-risques-de-tentions-a-anticiper/) in Kayes, Koulikoro, Ségou, and Mopti, and very severe deficits in the major pastoral areas of Tomboctou, Gao, and Kidal. Similarly, ponds and water reservoirs used for livestock watering have [**below-median water levels**](https://earlywarning.usgs.gov/fews/waterpoint/), with deficits ranging from 10 to 50 percent by locality. The atypically high pressure on pastoral resources will likely contribute to an early deterioration in livestock conditions in receiving areas, resulting in difficulties feeding livestock and consequently reducing livestock production.

fields.title: Sudan Key Message Update: As drought compounds conflict, the risk of Famine expands to parts of South Darfur, September 2026 - January 2027
fields.body:
**Key Messages**

- **Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes are expected to remain widespread across Greater Darfur, Greater Kordofan, and Blue Nile through January**. Some populations will likely continue to face Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5) in the worst conflict- and drought-affected locations, including Um Baru, Kernoi, and At-Tina of North Darfur; Dilling, Kadugli of South Kordofan and surrounding rural areas; El-Obeid and surrounding areas of North Kordofan; and among some internally displaced person (IDP) populations in Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan.
- Compared with the projection that FEWS NET issued in [**August**](https://fews.net/east-africa/sudan/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026), **more areas of Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan are now expected to remain in Emergency (IPC Phase 4) during the harvest period**, including additional areas of North Darfur (Dar As Salam, As Serief), West Darfur (Jebel Moon, Sirba), South Darfur (Sharg Aj-Jabal, Mershing, Nitega), East Darfur (Shia’ria) and parts of Soudari of North Kordofan. Drought has resulted in severely below-average harvest prospects and localized crop failure, while reduced agricultural labor opportunities, continued displacement, and sharply rising food prices will constrain household food access. In relatively calmer areas of southern Darfur and southern and eastern Greater Kordofan, below-average harvests will provide only limited seasonal relief, sustaining Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes.
- **The** [**risk of Famine (IPC Phase 5)** ](https://fews.net/sites/default/files/2025-09/Risk%20of%20Famine%20Explaner_0.pdf)**now extends to parts of South Darfur, including Sharg Aj-Jabal, also known as East Jebel Marra, where IDPs are concentrated.** Conflict has severely eroded household livelihoods, assets, mobility, and coping capacity, resulting in Emergency (IPC Phase 4) and Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5) outcomes. In two of four IDP camps assessed between late August and early September, Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) by weight-for-height exceeded the Famine (IPC Phase 5) threshold, while food consumption outcomes and crude and under-five mortality rates indicated Emergency (IPC Phase 4). Although these findings do not establish a Famine (IPC Phase 5) classification, there is little household capacity to cope with further deterioration in food access. If drought-related crop losses drive substantially more displacement into the area such that food from local production, markets, and humanitarian assistance falls far short of the combined population’s minimum caloric requirements, the share of households with extreme food consumption deficits would increase. Given extremely high acute malnutrition in two camps, mortality would likely rise rapidly, and Famine (IPC Phase 5) would become the most likely outcome.
- **The** [**risk of Famine (IPC Phase 5)**](https://fews.net/sites/default/files/2025-09/Risk%20of%20Famine%20Explaner_0.pdf) **also persists in previously identified areas of North Darfur (Um Baru, Kernoi, At-Tina, Kutum, rural Al Fasher, Melit, and Tawila) and Greater Kordofan (Dilling, Kadugli of South Kordofan and surrounding rural areas).** In these areas, the credible alternative scenario remains centered on conflict and exacerbated by anticipated below- to severely below-average harvests. Renewed escalation or severe restrictions on movement, trade, and humanitarian access, compounded by marginal to failed harvests, would likely further isolate households from food and income sources and drive starvation, acute malnutrition, and mortality above the Famine (IPC Phase 5) thresholds.
- **Harvests will range from below to severely below average across most of Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan.** [**September rainfall was severely below average**](https://data.chc.ucsb.edu/products/Early_Estimates/v3/Recent_Rainfall/with_forecast/moving_06pentad/africa/pngs/POA_09PentAccum_Current.png) across much of western Sudan, cementing the [**underperformance of the June-September seasonal rains** ](https://earlywarning.usgs.gov/fews/product/892/)and [**limiting crop recovery**](https://www.cropmonitor.org/crop-monitor-for-early-warning#section6), particularly across large agricultural areas of Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan. The severe dry conditions are also [**reducing pasture**](https://earlywarning.usgs.gov/fews/product/938/) and water access and driving early southward migration of pastoralists, increasing the risk of herder-farmer conflict as animals encroach on farmland. Livestock body conditions are also deteriorating, with reports of [**increased distress sales**](http://www.dabangasudan.org/en/all-news/article/centre-for-humanitarian-change-darfur-faces-deepening-humanitarian-crisis-as-rains-fail), falling livestock prices, and increased livestock deaths in parts of North and West Darfur. Key informants have also reported rising displacement from drought-affected areas to parts of Central and South Darfur, straining available local resources. **The overall below-average harvest, with crop failure across many areas, will sustain atypically high food assistance needs through the harvesting period and likely drive higher needs amid an anticipated** [**early start to the 2027 lean season**](https://fews.net/global/food-assistance-outlook-brief/september-2026/print)**.**
- **Conflict escalated considerably in September 2026 along the major front lines, with major territorial gains in North Kordofan and parts of southern Blue Nile driving new displacements and disrupting livelihoods.** The Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) launched its largest offensive since July in **North Kordofan**, seizing control of several key villages and [**Sodari town**](https://sudanwarmonitor.com/p/rsf-suffers-another-defeat-in-north-kordofan?utm_source=publication-search) (Sodari locality), while fighting intensified around Abu Qa’ud, Umm Sumaima, Kazgil, and Hamrat El-Sheikh. The fighting displaced civilians toward El-Obeid (North Kordofan), Ad-Dabbah (Northern), and other safer areas. In **Blue Nile**, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) built off territorial gains in late August in Geissan and [**Kurmuk**](https://sudanwarmonitor.com/p/surkum-garrison-capture), capturing[ **Jabal Kadam garrison**](https://sudanwarmonitor.com/p/rsf-seizes-another-strategic-army-garrison-in-blue-nile?utm_source=post-email-title&publication_id=1721782&post_id=216111483&utm_campaign=email-post-title&isFreemail=true&r=706u81&triedRedirect=true&utm_medium=email) on September 17. These gains put additional pressure on SAF positions around Ed-Damazine and the Roseires Dam near the Ethiopian border, underscoring Blue Nile's growing strategic significance. Along the front in **North and** **West Darfur**, fighting has continued between the RSF and SAF/Darfur Joint Forces (DJF) along the At Tina-Um Baru-Karnoi corridor and the Abu Qamra-Bir Saliba axis near the Chad border. Control of Kulbus and Bir Saliba (West Darfur) has remained highly[ **contested**](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10/has-the-sudanese-army-turned-the-page-on-control-of-western-sudan), with DJF ultimately maintaining momentum and capturing Abu Sorug on August 30. These gains have increased pressure on El-Geneina, raising the likelihood of intensified fighting as both sides prepare for a major confrontation.
- **Intercommunal conflict has also continued**, most notably between the Falata and Masalit tribes in [**Gereida Locality**](https://mailchi.mp/iom/dtm-sudan-flash-alert-gereida-gereida-town-south-darfur-update-001?e=5d1dd348a0) (South Darfur), and in the Kauda-Heiban area (South Kordofan) between SPLM-N forces and armed members of the Atoro/Otoro community. Clashes that escalated in mid-August in Kauda continued into early September, and included burning and looting of houses and villages, civilian deaths and displacement, and severe disruption to livelihoods. Drone attacks have also continued across the country, including a strike in[ **Um Rawaba**](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/sudans-rsf-steps-up-deadly-drone-attacks-frontline-cities-2026-09-24/) (North Kordofan) and on key infrastructure including the[ **Umm Alila fuel depot**](https://www.dabangasudan.org/en/all-news/article/rsf-drones-strike-el-gezira-fuel-depot-as-both-sides-report-shootdowns) east of Wad Madani (Al-Jazirah), [**Upper Atbara and Setit dam**](https://sudantribune.com/article/318785)complex (Gedaref), and the nearby Khashm al-Girba dam (Kassala). Overall, continued conflict and insecurity during September triggered new displacement of about 27,200individuals in North Kordofan, Blue Nile, South Kordofan, North Darfur, and South Darfur states.
- [**Staple food and fuel prices**](https://sudan.ifpri.info/essential-commodities-prices-and-availability-monitor/)continued to rise sharply across all markets in September 2026, driven by persistent inflation, conflict-related disruptions, supply chain constraints, liquidity shortages, and speculations around the expected below-average 2026 harvest. The SDG continued to weaken sharply against the USD, with average official and parallel market exchange rates up 22-29 percent from August and 64-123 percent higher than the same period last year. Fuel prices remained exceptionally high, 88 and 127 percent above February 2026 levels on the official and parallel markets, respectively, increasing transportation and marketing costs countrywide. Staple food prices continued to surge: millet, sorghum, and wheat grain prices increased 26-29 percent between July and August and again by 36-41 percent between August and September, while wheat flour increased 5 and 16 percent. The cumulative two-month increases have been sharpest in markets in Greater Darfur, reflecting the worst expected production losses and crop failure, tightening market supplies, and high transport costs, with little moderation in prices anticipated during the harvest period.
- **Health and nutrition outcomes continue to worsen across the country, driven by deteriorating food security and WASH and health care conditions.** Funding cuts have accelerated the near-collapse of the health care system, driving closures and downsizing of health facilities across Sudan and severely reducing access to lifesaving healthcare. The few remaining hospitals are increasingly overwhelmed; for example, in Tawila, [**Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF)**](https://www.msf.org/humanitarian-aid-cuts) operates the only 200-bed hospital serving around 600,000 displaced people, while cases of malaria and severe acute malnutrition continue to rise. With only 41 percent of the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan funded and an estimated 37 percent of health facilities out of service, millions face worsening barriers to assistance, healthcare, and nutrition services, contributing to deteriorating nutrition outcomes. In addition to the survey in IDP camps in Sharg Aj-Jabal, 20 SMART surveys were conducted during the lean season months between June and September across the country. Of these, 13 (65 percent) found GAM prevalence at Critical levels (15-29.9 percent), including six that exceeded 20 percent.
- **In August, humanitarian partners reached approximately 3.7 million people with** [**in-kind and cash assistance**](https://docs.wfp.org/api/documents/WFP-0000176140/download/)**, less than 20 percent of FEWS NET’s** [**estimated population in need**](https://fews.net/global/food-assistance-outlook-brief/september-2026)**.** The number reached in August represents an increase of about 8 percent in beneficiaries reached with in-kind assistance, predominantly in Greater Darfur, and an increase of 22 percent in beneficiaries reached with cash-based transfers compared to July. While August represents the largest reach for the third consecutive month, it remains deeply insufficient for the scale of need, particularly amid the expected severely below-average harvest prospects. Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan remain the center of WFP’s operational response, accounting for nearly three-quarters of all beneficiaries reached across Sudan during August.

fields.title: Ethiopia Key Message Update, September 2026 - January 2027: Conflict escalates rapidly in Tigray as delayed meher harvest extends lean season
fields.body:
**Key Messages**

- **Conflict escalated in northern Ethiopia in late September,** with clashes concentrated in areas of North Wello and Wag Himra (Amhara), Central, South, Southeast and East Tigray along the Tekeze River (Tigray), and Kilbet Rasu Zone (Afar). The ongoing conflict is concentrated primarily in urban areas and along roadways, disrupting fuel supplies, market activity, and transportation services and constraining household access to food and essential goods, particularly in conflict-affected areas. If the conflict persists at this intensity or worsens, food security conditions could deteriorate in affected areas as market supplies decline, access to cash and fuel remains constrained, and staple food prices rise further.
- **Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected to persist in areas of South and East Tigray, lowland woredas along the Tekeze River catchment, and in East and West Hararghe**, where [**seasonal rainfall totaled 50 percent or less of average**](https://edcintl.cr.usgs.gov/downloads/sciweb1/shared/fews/web/africa/east/pentadal/chirps/seasaccum/junsep/pctn/lta/graphics/ea_chirps_seasaccum_pctn_junsep_202653_lta.png) in the worst-affected areas, constraining crop production and therefore food access. The upcoming *meher* harvest is expected to be below average, with delayed crop development in some areas and [**crop failure in others**](https://edcintl.cr.usgs.gov/downloads/sciweb1/shared/fews/web/africa/east/dekadal/wrsi-chirps-etos/eastl/do/graphics/wsel202627do.png), limiting the harvest’s ability to improve household access to food. In areas of northern Ethiopia, the recent escalation in conflict is adding further pressure and disruptions to markets, transport, and livelihood activities. Elsewhere in northern and southern *meher*-dependent areas, the below-average *meher* harvest is expected to improve food and income access for poor households, supporting improvement to **Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes in many areas where rainfall has been adequate for crop production**.
- **Delayed crop development in parts of northern Ethiopia is postponing the harvest and extending the lean season.** In Tigray, many *meher* crops remain in the [**late growing and flowering stages**](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/636c12f7f9c2561de642a866/t/6aa01f725d9dbb1334be6449/1788878707573/EarlyWarning_CropMonitor_202609.pdf), when they would typically be approaching or entering the harvesting stage. This delay of at least one month postpones the green harvest, which typically begins in September, keeping poor households reliant on market purchases longer than usual amid limited purchasing power. In conflict-affected northern areas, recent conflict is likely to add further pressure by temporarily disrupting access to fields and, in some locations, delaying or constraining harvesting activities.
- **Nationally, the** ***meher*** **harvest will most likely be below average, driven by severe** ***meher*** **production deficits in drought-affected lowlands of northern and eastern Ethiopia,** with the largest deficits concentrated in parts of Tigray, Amhara, and Oromia, despite late-season rainfall improving *meher* harvest expectations in western surplus-producing areas\*\*.\*\* The most affected areas include South, East, and Central of Tigray; Wag Himra, North Gondar and North Wello of Amhara; and East and West Hararghe of Oromia. Production losses are estimated at more than 40 percent in East and West Hararghe. The poor sorghum harvest in North Wello Zone of Amhara and South Tigray has reportedly led to a significant reduction in agricultural labor opportunities for both local workers and seasonal migrants from the highlands.
- **Staple food supplies remain below average, driving high food prices amid seasonally high demand, high transportation costs, and broader macroeconomic pressures.** In August 2026, white sorghum prices in Sekota were 50 percent higher than in August 2025 and nearly 75 percent above the five-year average. In East Hararghe, key informants report that maize and sorghum prices rose sharply from August to September. Price increases reflect reduced supply associated with delays in the *meher* harvest and rising and already high fuel costs that constrain the movement of goods. Recent conflict-related disruptions to markets, transport, and supply routes in northern areas are likely adding further pressure on staple food availability and prices.
- [**Limited to no rainfall across most of Afar**](https://edcintl.cr.usgs.gov/downloads/sciweb1/shared/fews/web/africa/east/pentadal/chirps/seasaccum/junsep/total/graphics/ea_chirps_seasaccum_total_junsep_202654.png) **during the July to September** ***karan/karma*** **rain season has severely reduced** [**pasture regeneration, with severely dry conditions**](https://edcintl.cr.usgs.gov/downloads/sciweb1/shared/fews/web/africa/east/pentadal/eviirs/ndvi/percentofmean/graphics/ea2654pct.png)**.** Pasture and water availability are of particular concern in northern Afar, particularly in Teru, Kori, and Elidar Zones, raising the risk of atypically early deterioration in livestock body conditions and migration if forecast unseasonal rainfall fails to materialize\*\*.\*\* Livestock body conditions are currently slightly below normal, while no significant atypical livestock movement has been reported to date, and livestock prices remain broadly stable. However, conflict-related disruptions to livestock trade and market access are likely to place downward pressure on livestock prices by limiting traders’ ability to reach affected areas and move animals to market.
- **Most south and southeast pastoral areas are experiencing hot, dry conditions associated with the seasonal dry period.** Moisture from the March to May 2026 *gu/genna* rainy season rapidly depleted as above-average temperatures [**desiccated pasture**](https://edcintl.cr.usgs.gov/downloads/sciweb1/shared/fews/web/africa/east/pentadal/eviirs/ndvi/percentofmean/graphics/ea2654pct.png) and accelerated water loss, increasing the concentration of livestock on limited available fodder and water resources in September. The [**October to December** ***deyr/hageya*** **rains**](https://fews.net/global/seasonal-forecast-monthly-briefing/september-2026/print) are expected to improve pasture, water availability, and livestock conditions, although forecast localized riverine and flash flooding could limit recovery in flood-affected areas.
- **Humanitarian food assistance resumed in Tigray in July 2026, targeting over 1.1 million people. Most of those targeted are internally displaced populations.** Food distributions are complete, while cash distributions are ongoing, with more than 60 percent of the planned caseload reached at the end of August; however, conflict is likely disrupting food assistance distributions. In East Hararghe Zone, the Hararghe Catholic Secretariat, with support from the Joint Emergency Operation (JEOP), provided humanitarian assistance to approximately 223,000 people across seven *woredas* in August 2026.

Disclaimer: *The analysis in this report reflects information available as of September 30, 2026. While it incorporates the initial escalation of conflict in northern Ethiopia beginning in late September, the situation has continued to evolve rapidly. Subsequent developments and the impacts of the escalation on acute food insecurity will become available after October 31, 2026.*

fields.title: Syria Key Message Update: Fuel price increase erodes purchasing power as winter costs and lean season approach, September 2026 - January 2027
fields.body:
## Key Messages

- **Widespread Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are ongoing in Northeast (NES) and Northwest (NWS) Syria, as a mid-September fuel price increase erodes household purchasing power well ahead of the January lean season**. On September 13, diesel prices [**rose by 40 percent**](https://www.enabbaladi.net/824871/...) to 175 SYP/liter, raising [**transport fares**](https://www.enabbaladi.net/824978/...) and food prices. The increase sparked [**the most widespread protests**](https://acleddata.com/expert-comment/what-behind-syrias-fuel-price-protests) since the fall of the al-Assad government, with demonstrators blocking major highways and oil tanker routes in several governorates. After [**subsidized diesel for bakeries and mills stopped**](https://www.enabbaladi.net/822934/%d8%a8%d8%b9%d8%af-%d8%a7%d9%86%d8%aa%d9%87%d8%a7%d8%a1-%d8%ad%d8%b5%d8%a9-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%ac%d8%b2%d9%8a%d8%b1%d8%a9-%d8%a7%d9%84%d9%85%d8%a7%d8%b2%d9%88%d8%aa-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%ae%d8%af%d9%85/) on August 28, the price of a loaf of bread in Qamishli [**rose by 45 percent**](https://7al.net/article/%d8%b3%d8%b9%d8%b1-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%ae%d8%a8%d8%b2-3/), and [**many bakeries across Al-Hasakah halted production**](https://7al.net/article/%d8%b1%d8%ba%d9%8a%d9%81-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%ae%d8%a8%d8%b2-%d8%a3%d9%88%d9%84-%d8%a7%d9%84%d9%85%d8%aa%d8%b6%d8%b1%d8%b1%d9%8a%d9%86-%d8%b9%d8%b4%d8%b1%d8%a7%d8%aa-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%a3%d9%81%d8%b1%d8%a7/) on September 15, while [**sugar and rice prices rose by 31 and 20 percent, respectively**](https://www.enabbaladi.net/826499/%d8%b1%d9%81%d8%b9-%d8%a3%d8%b3%d8%b9%d8%a7%d8%b1-%d8%a7%d9%84%d9%85%d8%ad%d8%b1%d9%88%d9%82%d8%a7%d8%aa-%d9%8a%d9%81%d8%a7%d9%82%d9%85-%d8%a3%d8%b2%d9%85%d8%a9-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%ba%d9%84%d8%a7%d8%a1/) in Damascus, reducing access to a key staple for poor households. In response to the protests, the government announced a [**lower 115 SYP/liter tier for heating and agriculture**](https://www.enabbaladi.net/825444/%d9%88%d8%b2%d9%8a%d8%b1-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%b7%d8%a7%d9%82%d8%a9-%d9%8a%d8%b9%d9%84%d9%86-%d8%b7%d8%b1%d8%ad-%d8%ab%d9%84%d8%a7%d8%ab%d8%a9-%d8%a3%d9%86%d9%88%d8%a7%d8%b9-%d9%85%d9%86-%d8%a7%d9%84%d9%85/) on September 17, although it has not yet been implemented.
- **Delayed payments and rising production costs are reducing income across NES, likely sustaining Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes through January 2027 among poor households that depend on agricultural labor.** The three NES governorates produced about two-thirds of Syria's wheat last season, yet many farmers [**remain unpaid, with dues not scheduled to be cleared until the end of November**](https://www.enabbaladi.net/826494/%d9%85%d8%b2%d8%a7%d8%b1%d8%b9%d9%88-%d8%a7%d9%84%d9%82%d9%85%d8%ad-%d9%8a%d9%86%d8%aa%d8%b8%d8%b1%d9%88%d9%86-%d8%a3%d8%ab%d9%85%d8%a7%d9%86-%d9%85%d8%ad%d8%a7%d8%b5%d9%8a%d9%84%d9%87%d9%85/), and most borrowed to finance inputs. In Al-Hasakah, the largest producer, land preparation [**had not begun on a broad scale by late September**](https://7al.net/article/%d8%a3%d9%8a%d9%86-%d8%b0%d9%87%d8%a8%d8%aa-%d9%85%d8%b3%d8%aa%d8%ad%d9%82%d8%a7%d8%aa-%d8%a7%d9%84%d9%82%d9%85%d8%ad%d8%9f-%d9%85%d8%b2%d8%a7%d8%b1%d8%b9%d9%88-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%ad%d8%b3%d9%83%d8%a9/), as farmers lacked cash for fuel and hired labor. Harvest labor is also declining. In Ar-Raqqa, cotton area has [**fallen by 80 percent compared with previous years**](https://www.enabbaladi.net/825795/%d9%85%d8%b2%d8%a7%d8%b1%d8%b9%d9%88-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%b1%d9%82%d8%a9-%d9%8a%d8%a8%d8%af%d8%a4%d9%88%d9%86-%d8%ac%d9%86%d9%8a-%d8%a7%d9%84%d9%82%d8%b7%d9%86-%d9%87%d9%88%d8%a7%d8%ac%d8%b3-%d8%a7%d9%84/) due to high costs and uncertain marketing, reducing picking work through November. Non-agricultural income is also under pressure, as some public employees in Deir ez-Zor [**have gone unpaid for more than four months**](https://7al.net/article/%d8%a5%d8%b6%d8%b1%d8%a7%d8%a8-%d8%b9%d9%85%d8%a7%d9%84-%d9%83%d9%87%d8%b1%d8%a8%d8%a7%d8%a1-%d8%af%d9%8a%d8%b1-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%b2%d9%88%d8%b1-%d8%a7%d8%ad%d8%aa%d8%ac%d8%a7%d8%ac%d8%a7%d9%8b-%d8%b9/). Together, these delays reduce seasonal income just as higher fuel prices raise transport and food costs.
- **Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected to persist in NES through January 2027, with some of the poorest households — including camp-based internally displaced persons (IDPs) and returnees without land or livestock — likely facing large food consumption gaps consistent with Emergency (IPC Phase 4) as the loss of subsidized diesel raises bread prices and delays winter planting**. Some poor households are increasingly relying on children's earnings, including income from [**waste picking**](https://www.enabbaladi.net/824640/%d9%86%d8%a8%d9%91%d8%a7%d8%b4%d9%88-%d8%a7%d9%84%d9%82%d9%85%d8%a7%d9%85%d8%a9-%d8%a8%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%ad%d8%b3%d9%83%d8%a9-%d8%a3%d8%b7%d9%81%d8%a7%d9%84-%d9%8a%d9%86%d9%87%d8%b4%d9%87%d9%85/), indicating that other coping options are becoming more constrained while worst-off households are already [**relying on severe coping strategies, such as debt, child labor, and child marriage**](https://repository.impact-initiatives.org/document/impact/8a76a009/Northeast_Syria_Needs_Update_Al-Hasakeh_FINAL.pdf), to meet food needs. High market dependence makes these households particularly vulnerable to higher food prices, while declining assistance is likely to further constrain access to food among [**IDPs in informal camps, such as the nearly 10,000 in Ar-Raqqa**](https://damapost.com/09/09/2026/%d9%85%d8%ae%d9%8a%d9%85%d8%a7-%d8%b3%d9%87%d9%84%d8%a9-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%a8%d9%86%d8%a7%d8%aa-%d9%88%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%a8%d9%8a%d8%aa-%d8%a7%d9%84%d9%8a%d9%88%d9%86%d8%a7%d9%86%d9%8a/125881/).
- **Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected to persist in NWS through January 2027, with the poorest camp-based IDPs and returnees likely facing large food consumption gaps consistent with Emergency (IPC Phase 4) due to asset losses, limited income-earning opportunities, and rising winter expenditures.** Returns from camps are accelerating, but many returnees [**live in tents beside their destroyed homes**](https://ultrasyria.ultrasawt.com/%D9%8A%D8%B9%D9%88%D8%AF%D9%88%D9%86-%D8%A5%D9%84%D9%89-%D9%85%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%B2%D9%84%D9%87%D9%85-%D9%84%D9%8A%D9%82%D9%8A%D9%85%D9%88%D8%A7-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AE%D9%8A%D8%A7%D9%85-%D9%81%D9%88%D9%82-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D9%86%D9%82%D8%A7%D8%B6/%D9%87%D8%AF%D9%89-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%83%D9%84%D9%8A%D8%A8/%D9%85%D8%AC%D8%AA%D9%85%D8%B9-%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%82%D8%AA%D8%B5%D8%A7%D8%AF) where rubble and landmines prevent them from resuming farming and leave them dependent on casual labor and market purchases. [**At least 816,760 IDPs remain in camps in NWS**](https://thawra.sy/report/%d8%a7%d9%84%d9%85%d8%ae%d9%8a%d9%85%d8%a7%d8%aa-%d9%88%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%a3%d9%86%d9%82%d8%a7%d8%b6-%d9%88%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%a3%d9%84%d8%ba%d8%a7%d9%85-%d8%b3%d8%aa%d8%a9-%d9%85%d9%84%d9%81%d8%a7%d8%aa/) and depend on labor income and markets to meet food needs. As winter begins, rising shelter and heating costs will compete more directly with food expenditures for both groups. In Hama, [**surplus summer vegetable production pushed cucumber prices down to 7 SYP/kg**](https://aliqtisadiya.com/agriculture-livestock/food-security/hama-agricultural-plan-production-surplus-fails-farmers-consumers/), leading some farmers to discard produce, while higher fuel prices have disrupted [**transport and wholesale trade**](https://www.alainsyria.com/article/3321). Seasonal harvest work elsewhere in Idlib is expected to provide some income beginning in October, but opportunities will likely be short term. Without land or livestock, asset-poor IDPs and returnees will remain highly dependent on casual labor and market purchases, and rising heating costs are likely to further widen their food consumption gaps.
- **Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes are expected to continue in Tartus through January 2027, while Latakia is expected to deteriorate to Crisis (IPC Phase 3) as seasonal income from tourism and fishing declines**. In [**Tartus**](https://sana.sy/locals/2571542/), olive production is expected to reach 127,000 metric tons (MT), compared with 10,000 MT last season and 32,000 MT in 2024. Combined with year-round agricultural income sources, the strong olive harvest is expected to help most poor households maintain minimally adequate food consumption. In Latakia, poor households have fewer seasonal income-earning opportunities and rely more heavily on tourism and fishing, which typically decline after the summer season. Tobacco farmers face additional pressure, with some [**reportedly waiting 11 months for payment**](https://www.enabbaladi.net/824701/%d9%85%d8%b2%d8%a7%d8%b1%d8%b9%d9%88%d9%86-%d9%8a%d8%b4%d8%aa%d9%83%d9%88%d9%86-%d8%aa%d8%a3%d8%ae%d8%b1-%d8%aa%d8%b3%d9%84%d9%8a%d9%85-%d8%ab%d9%85%d9%86-%d9%85%d8%ad%d8%a7%d8%b5%d9%8a%d9%84%d9%87/) and borrowing to finance planting, increasing debt repayment obligations that are likely to compete with winter food purchases. As seasonal income declines and debt obligations remain elevated, poor households in Latakia are likely to face increasing difficulty meeting their food and essential non-food needs.
- **Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes are expected to persist across southern Syria through January 2027, as most poor households are likely to maintain minimally adequate food consumption but remain unable to afford some essential non-food expenditures, particularly water.** In [**Daraa**](https://thawra.sy/report/%d9%85%d8%a7%d8%b0%d8%a7-%d9%8a%d8%ad%d8%af%d8%ab-%d9%84%d9%84%d9%85%d9%8a%d8%a7%d9%87-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%ac%d9%88%d9%81%d9%8a%d8%a9-%d9%81%d9%8a-%d8%af%d8%b1%d8%b9%d8%a7/), drought and groundwater over-extraction have reduced main spring flows by 86 percent, and 60 percent of the population reportedly receives only 0-25 liters of water per person per day. Increasing reliance on trucked water, combined with a 60 percent increase in tanker prices, is raising household water expenditures as deeper groundwater and more distant sources increase pumping and transport costs, diverting income from food and other essential needs. In Quneitra and parts of Daraa, intensifying [**Israeli military activity continues**](https://www.enabbaladi.net/823352/%d8%aa%d9%82%d8%b1%d9%8a%d8%b1-%d8%ad%d9%82%d9%88%d9%82%d9%8a267-%d8%a7%d9%86%d8%aa%d9%87%d8%a7%d9%83%d9%8b%d8%a7-%d8%a5%d8%b3%d8%b1%d8%a7%d8%a6%d9%8a%d9%84%d9%8a%d9%8b%d8%a7-%d8%af%d8%a7%d8%ae%d9%84/) to restrict access to farmland and grazing areas, further constraining agricultural and livestock livelihoods. Wholesale traders in As-Suwayda reportedly [**went on strike on September 7 over checkpoint fees and delays**](https://7al.net/article/%d8%a5%d8%b6%d8%b1%d8%a7%d8%a8-%d8%aa%d8%ac%d8%a7%d8%b1-%d8%b3%d9%88%d9%82-%d8%a7%d9%84%d9%87%d8%a7%d9%84-%d9%81%d9%8a-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%b3%d9%88%d9%8a%d8%af%d8%a7%d8%a1-%d8%a7%d8%ad%d8%aa%d8%ac%d8%a7/), although authorities have denied the allegations. If restrictions on incoming goods persist and contribute to sustained price increases, poor and displaced households could deteriorate to Crisis (IPC Phase 3).

fields.title: Lesotho: Key Message Update - Land preparation ongoing at average levels following agricultural input subsidies, September 2026 - January 2027
fields.body:
**Key Messages**

- **As food stocks begin to decline following a below-average 2026 harvest, Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes are expected to persist in the Southern Lowlands, Senqu River Valley, and Mountain regions** through January 2027, with some poor households in Crisis (IPC Phase 3). As food stocks deplete, households are likely to become increasingly market-reliant for food. Purchasing power is likely to further erode beginning in October, as income-earning opportunities, local brew sales, and remittances decline. Conversely, **Minimal (IPC Phase 1) outcomes are anticipated to persist through January in the Northern Lowlands and Foothills**, supported by an average harvest and adequate access to food stocks.
- The [**2026 maize harvest**](https://www.bos.gov.ls/Publications.htm) is complete countrywide. The Lesotho Bureau of Statistics estimates national production at 30 percent below last year and 55 percent below the five-year average, with below-average harvests in the Mountains, Senqu River Valley, and Southern Lowlands, and average harvests elsewhere. The shortfall follows heavy rains in April and May that caused waterlogging and delayed harvesting in the Senqu River Valley and Foothills.
- The [**October 2026 to March 2027 rainy season**](https://psl.noaa.gov/cgi-bin/forecasts/s2s_C3S_monthly_to_seasonal/getC3Sm2sImage.pl?currMMYYYY=092026&lead=06&model=multimodel&region=southern_africa&var=tprate&stat=poa_regular&MonOrSeas=monthly) is likely to begin late and be below-average, influenced by forecast strong El Niño conditions. Below-average rainfall and increased dry spells are expected to constrain crop development and yields, particularly for maize, which is highly sensitive to dry conditions.
- According to the Department of Crops, land preparation is underway. In the Mountains, activities began on time and are progressing typically, while in the Senqu River Valley, Foothills, Northern Lowlands, and Southern Lowlands, land preparation began atypically late, starting one month late in September, but is progressing steadily and is expected to support a timely start to planting. Agricultural inputs, including seed and fertilizer, are available through the government's 2026/27 Input Support Programme, which subsidizes seed and fertilizer prices by 70 and 80 percent, respectively. These subsidies have sharply reduced production costs and improved input access. Combined with [**favorable soil moisture**](https://edcintl.cr.usgs.gov/downloads/sciweb1/shared/fews/web/africa/southern/monthly/soilmoisture/sm_0_10cm/sm_pct_anomaly/graphics/sa_monthly_fldas_soilmoi00_10cm_tavg_pctanom_2608.png) following [**rainfall in August and September**](https://data.chc.ucsb.edu/products/Early_Estimates/v3/Recent_Rainfall/observed/moving_12pentad/africa_southern/pngs/POA_12PentAccum_Current.png), area planted is expected to be average despite the likelihood of a poor start of the rainy season and the atypically late start to land preparation in some areas.
- Staple food prices are expected to remain stable and below last year through the projection period, supported by continued imports from South Africa and available carryover stocks, despite below-average domestic production. However, poor households that experienced below-average harvests are likely to deplete their own-produced food stocks atypically early, beginning in September, increasing reliance on market purchases ahead of the January 2027 lean season.

fields.title: Pakistan: Key Message Update - High food prices and below-average kharif harvest expected to drive Crisis outcomes, September 2026 - January 2027
fields.body:
**Key Messages**

- **Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are anticipated in Balochistan, Sindh, and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) provinces through at least January 2027 as poor households deplete own-produced** ***rabi*** **wheat stocks and the** ***kharif*** **harvest will most likely be insufficient to replenish household food stocks.** The *kharif* harvest and *rabi* land preparation from October to December are expected to provide some income-earning opportunities ahead of the lean season beginning in January. However, income from these opportunities is expected to be below average, following the poor [**June to September monsoon season**](https://data.chc.ucsb.edu/products/Early_Estimates/v3/Seasonal_Rainfall/observed/asia_central_and_south/jun_to_sep/pngs/POA_Current.png) and the resulting below-average *kharif* harvest. As household food stocks deplete, households are expected to become increasingly market dependent, but below-average income from labor is expected to limit their ability to purchase sufficient food amid high food prices.
- **Stressed (IPC Phase 2) and Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are anticipated to continue through January 2027 in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) and Gilgit-Baltistan (GB) regions.** As winter begins in December, seasonal road closures, high food and transportation costs, and seasonal declines in livelihood activities are anticipated to limit household access to food and income, resulting in an expansion of Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes, mainly in GB Region.
- [**June to September monsoon rainfall**](https://data.chc.ucsb.edu/products/Early_Estimates/v3/Seasonal_Rainfall/observed/asia_central_and_south/jun_to_sep/pngs/POA_Current.png) was significantly below average in Balochistan, Sindh, and parts of Punjab and KP provinces, while average to above average in the rest of the country. Below-average rainfall in southern regions has driven moisture stress, increasing irrigation demand and driving greater groundwater extraction where canal water supplies are insufficient. [**Winter precipitation**](https://fews.net/global/seasonal-forecast-monthly-briefing/september-2026), beginning in December 2026, is expected to be average countrywide, with the potential for above-average precipitation in localized areas, supporting *rabi* land preparation and planting, and weeding.
- The 2026 *kharif* harvest is expected to be below last year, driven by below-average monsoon rainfall from June to September and persistent irrigation water shortages that reduced area planted for rice, particularly in Sindh and Balochistan provinces. As a result, poor farming households, including smallholder farmers and sharecroppers, are expected to face reduced own-produced food and access to income-earning opportunities, increasing market dependence and constraining food access.
- [**Lumpy skin disease (LSD)**](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/lsdv_fadprep_ee.pdf#%5B%7B%22num%22%3A17%2C%22gen%22%3A0%7D%2C%7B%22name%22%3A%22XYZ%22%7D%2C70%2C720%2C0%5D) and [**foot-and-mouth disease (FMD)**](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/cattle/foot-and-mouth) are [**spreading** ](https://www.dawn.com/news/2026238)across parts of KP Province, particularly in Bannu, Nowshera, Swabi, Lower Dir, and Dera Ismail Khan (DI Khan) districts, with the [**highest mortality reported in DI Khan and Nowshera**](https://www.24newshd.tv/15-Sep-2026/several-cattle-die-lumpy-skin-disease-hits-several-kp-districts). In Balochistan Province, LSD cases are widespread, particularly in Sherani, Killa Saifullah, Sibi, Musakhel, Kech, Loralai, and Barkhan districts. While the outbreaks have remained localized at the district level, livestock deaths and reduced productivity among infected animals are expected to lower income for livestock-reliant households in these districts.
- According to the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics, in the Lahore reference market, wheat flour prices in August were 51 percent above last year and 40 percent above the five-year average. High prices are driven by high fuel and transportation costs, private-sector stockholding, and market grain prices exceeding the government's procurement price. The federal government has[ **released public stocks**](https://mettisglobal.news/DPM-orders-immediate-wheat-release-reaffirms-1m-tonne-import-plan-63202) to the provinces and fast-tracked the emergency import of one million metric tons of wheat, with an initial 750,000 metric tons scheduled to arrive by November 2026. These interventions are expected to stabilize prices for only one to three months. As household and government stocks decline during the October to December planting period, prices are expected to remain above average through January, particularly in the wheat deficit-producing provinces of KP, Balochistan, and Sindh, as well as AJK and GB regions.

fields.title: Проучване на безопасността в местата за настаняване с особено внимание на насилието, основано на пол (GBV) [BG]
fields.body:
ВЪВЕДЕНИЕ

Благодарение на дългогодишния си глобален опит в различни ситуации на разселване, ВКБООН признава, че насилието срещу жени и момичета, както и срещу други лица с комбинирани уязвимости, се среща във всички общества и контексти, включително в ситуации на разселване, и че то остава значително недокладвано поради бариери като страх, стигма, липса на доверие, отношения на зависимост и ограничен достъп до услуги. Поради тази причина всеки носи отговорност да идентифицира и намалява такива рискове в рамките на съответната си сфера на дейност, въз основа на нуждите и преживяванията на засегнатите общности. Оценката на безопасността не е предназначена да документира, проверява или търси доказателства за отделни инциденти. По-скоро тя предоставя безопасен и етичен начин да се разберат възприятията за безопасност, да се идентифицират обстоятелствените и структурните фактори, които могат да доведат до повишаване на риска от насилие, и да се съберат гледните точки на общността относно мерки, които могат да укрепят закрилата, да намалят рисковете и да подобрят достъпа до услуги за подкрепа. Като се фокусира върху рисковите фактори, опасенията за безопасността и решенията, инициирани от общността, оценки на безопасността на ВКБООН имат за цел да събере доказателства за превенция и намаляване на риска, като същевременно избягват подходи, които биха могли да изложат лицата на опасност или да наложат натиск върху преживялите насилие да разкриват преживяното. Те служат също като платформа за укрепване на сътрудничеството между общностите, властите, доставчиците на услуги и хуманитарните организации с цел подобряване на механизмите за превенция, реагиране и отчетност.

Настоящото проучване относно безопасността в местата за настаняване на принудително разселени лица в България, с особен акцент върху рисковете от насилие срещу жени и други хора с комбинирани уязвимости, беше проведено в съответствие с установената от ВКБООН международна рамка за подобни изследвания, с подкрепата на Държавната агенция за бежанците и на Дирекцията „Миграция“. Беше използвана триангулация от смесени методи за събиране на данни: кабинетно проучване на статистически данни и нормативни документи; посещения на място за оценка на безопасността в местата за настаняване; както и дискусии във фокус групи и интервюта с експерти. Бяха посетени дванадесет места за настаняване и два центъра за закрила и приобщаване „Компас“, като бяха събрани мненията на 150 души.

Събраните данни показват, че рискът от насилие, основано на пола, не е функция на „опасни лица“, а на опасни условия. Жените, децата и лицата от ЛГБТИК+ общността не търсят специално отношение, а предвидимост, сигурност, достойнство и правото на нормален живот. Бяха идентифицирани скрити рискове от конфликти, които се пренасят при принудително разселване и се проявяват в приемащата среда. Някои от тях имат социалнополитически произход и могат да ескалират до физическа агресия между групи с различен произход.

Други рискове са свързани с утвърдени модели на тежко насилие, включително насилие, основано на пола, извършвано в името на „честта“. Тези практики представляват сериозно нарушение на правата на човека и изискват ясна идентификация, превенция и специализирана институционална реакция, без да се допуска тяхното културно оправдаване или нормализиране.

fields.title: L’union Africaine, championne de la santé maternelle et infantile: Feuille de route sur la santé reproductive, maternelle, néonatale, infantile et adolescente (2026-2030)
fields.body:
**CHAPITRE 1 : INTRODUCTION ET CONTEXTE**

**1.1 Contexte**

L’Union africaine (UA) a nommé S.E. Dr Samia Suluhu Hassan, Présidente de la République-Unie de Tanzanie, « Championne de l’UA pour la santé maternelle et infantile » lors de l’Assemblée des Chefs d’État et de gouvernement de l’UA de février 2026 (Décision AU/Dec.25(XXXIX)). La Championne de l’UA pour la santé maternelle et infantile a pour objectif de mobiliser un leadership politique de haut niveau et des actions de plaidoyer, des investissements durables et une forte responsabilisation afin d’accélérer les progrès visant à mettre fin aux décès évitables chez les mères, les nouveau-nés, les enfants et les adolescents à travers l’Afrique. Une liste consolidée des acronymes utilisés dans la Feuille de route figure à l’annexe A. Bien que des progrès significatifs aient été réalisés au cours des deux dernières décennies, l’Afrique continue de supporter une part disproportionnée du fardeau mondial de la mortalité maternelle, néonatale et infantile, ce qui souligne la nécessité d’un engagement politique plus fort, d’une action coordonnée et d’investissements soutenus.

fields.title: Continental Roadmap on Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health (2026-2030) [EN/POR]
fields.body:
## **EXECUTIVE SUMMARY**

Africa has made important gains in the health and survival of women and children, but progress remains too slow and unequal to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals by 2030. The continent accounts for approximately 70% of global maternal deaths, nearly half of deaths among children under five, nearly half of global stillbirths, and more than half of the world’s zero-dose children. Most are preventable. The priority is to convert existing evidence, policies and proven interventions into sustained political commitment, adequate financing and quality services for populations and geographies carrying the greatest burden.

The appointment of H.E. Dr. Samia Suluhu Hassan, President of the United Republic of Tanzania, as African Union Champion for Maternal and Child Health provides a high-level platform to accelerate this transition from commitment to results. The AU Champion Roadmap for RMNCAH 2026–2030 is a continental political and delivery-acceleration framework that strengthens national plans and continental commitments rather than creating a new policy or parallel implementation system.

At its centre are the Three Zeros: Zero Home Delivery, with every birth managed by skilled health personnel in a properly equipped medical environment; Zero Preventable Maternal and Newborn Deaths, so preventable deaths are no longer accepted as inevitable and every death informs corrective action; and Zero Unvaccinated Children, so every child is identified, reached and protected through age-appropriate immunisation, with particular focus on zero-dose children. Adolescent health and wellbeing cut across all three.

The Roadmap advances this promise through three mutually reinforcing Strategic Objectives. SO1 mobilises political leadership and partnerships for accountability through high-level advocacy, evidence and convening. SO2 mobilises and aligns investment and delivery systems by strengthening implementation-ready Integrated RMNCAH Investment Cases, linking priorities to national budgets, aligning domestic and partner financing, and reinforcing product security, pooled procurement, African manufacturing and PHC digitalisation. SO3 accelerates country implementation of proven high-impact interventions across the continuum of reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health, including SRH, adolescent and youth-responsive health, nutrition across the life course, maternal and newborn survival, stillbirth prevention, child health and immunisation, supported by a competent and retained workforce, community systems, quality care, functional referral and South–South learning.

Implementation remains Member State-owned and led. All 55 AU Member States participate, with intensified support differentiated by burden, SDG trajectory, equity and service gaps, fragility and conflict-related disruption, financing and implementation constraints, and country demand and readiness. The AU MCH Champion provides political leadership and high-level accountability; the Champion Secretariat supports advocacy, commitment tracking, resource mobilisation and implementation oversight; Africa CDC leads continental technical coordination and country support; and partners align financing and technical assistance behind country-owned priorities.

Accountability will focus on results. A seven-indicator Presidential RMNCAH Scorecard will track the Three Zeros, maternal and newborn lifesaving service readiness and domestic financing for delivery, supported by the broader Continental RMNCAH Scorecard and Dashboard. By 2030, success will be judged by measurable progress across these headline indicators.
